impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the United States in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling based on a prior class action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501's six-year statute of limitations for Tucker Act claims is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc. implicitly overruled a portion of the Federal Circuit's prior holding in Bright v. United States. This means participation in a prior class action does not toll the limitations period for individual suits against the government in the Court of Federal Claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides certainty for the government as defendant that Tucker Act claims must be individually filed within the statutory period, preventing stale claims from being revived through class action tolling.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and individuals with financial claims against the U.S. government (including contract disputes, takings, and tax refunds) cannot rely on a pending class action to preserve their individual right to sue, creating risk of time-barred claims if they do not independently file within six years.

impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether, under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2), a reference patent's entitlement to its provisional application's filing date for prior art purposes requires that at least one claim of the non-provisional patent be supported by the provisional application's written description, as required under pre-AIA law by Dynamic Drinkware.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the PTAB's decision that found Dental Monitoring's patent claims obvious, taking up the significant question of whether the Dynamic Drinkware written description analysis applies under the AIA's prior art framework. The Board had relied on its Penumbra precedent to hold that only 'ministerial requirements' need be met for a reference to claim its provisional filing date. The outcome will determine the scope of prior art available in IPR proceedings under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: If Dynamic Drinkware's stricter standard applies under the AIA, patent owners will benefit from a narrower universe of prior art, as challenger references would need to demonstrate written description support in provisional applications to claim earlier priority dates.
impacts.negativeImplications: If Dynamic Drinkware applies, petitioners in IPR proceedings face a higher burden to establish that reference patents qualify as prior art based on provisional filing dates, potentially making it harder and more expensive to challenge patent validity.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement for method-of-treatment patent claims permits broad functional genus claims where the specification does not enable the full scope of antibodies encompassed by the claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied Eli Lilly's petition for rehearing en banc on the enablement standard for method claims involving anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headaches. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding sustains overly broad method claims and is contrary to Supreme Court enablement precedent. The denial preserves the panel's more permissive enablement standard for method claims in the pharmaceutical and biologics space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders benefit from a more permissive enablement standard for method-of-treatment claims, allowing broader patent protection for therapeutic antibody methods without needing to enable every possible antibody within the claimed genus.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face broader patent barriers to market entry, as the decision sustains broad method-of-treatment claims that may block development of alternative antibodies falling within broadly claimed genera.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement when calculating copyright infringement damages, and what constitutes a legally permissible 'book of wisdom' analysis in a hypothetical negotiation for government copyright infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's decision to use a hypothetical negotiation rather than existing license terms to assess copyright infringement damages for the government's unauthorized copying of TETRA software, but vacated in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. The case establishes that courts are not compelled to defer to existing license rates when calculating infringement damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders suing the government retain flexibility in damages theories, as courts may use hypothetical negotiations rather than being bound by pre-existing license rates that may undervalue the IP.
impacts.negativeImplications: The government and licensees benefit from limits on the 'book of wisdom' doctrine, as the court found the trial court improperly used post-infringement information and assessed non-compensatory damages, potentially reducing damage awards in future copyright infringement cases.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert testimony and in its assessment of breach of contract damages arising from software misappropriation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the breach of contract damages ruling and reinstated the jury's award. The court affirmed the district court's denial of Ford's JMOL on trade secret misappropriation liability, upholding the finding that Ford misappropriated Versata's automotive configuration software trade secrets.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and trade secret owners benefit from the court's affirmation of liability for misappropriation of combination trade secrets in complex software, and from the reinstatement of the jury's breach of contract damages award.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop competing products after licensing third-party software face significant trade secret misappropriation liability risk, even where the district court initially excluded the plaintiff's primary damages theory. The remand for reconsideration of damages models may lead to larger awards.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to patent enforcement constituted ceasing business operations triggering automatic termination of the agreement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal of TexasLDPC's patent infringement suit against Broadcom, holding that shifting from commercialization to patent enforcement did not constitute ceasing business operations under the license agreement, and that the agreement conveyed all substantial rights making TexasLDPC the effective patent owner entitled to sue without joining the university licensor. This clarifies the rights of exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from confirmation that enforcement-focused business models do not trigger termination clauses, and that comprehensive exclusive licenses can convey sufficient rights to sue independently without the patent owner.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose the defense of challenging standing based on the licensee's shift to enforcement rather than commercialization, potentially making it harder to dismiss suits by patent assertion entities on standing grounds.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for the '509 and '922 patent claims, in a case involving communication technology used in television broadcasting. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. This decision provides important guidance on the Alice/Mayo framework as applied to digital communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: The affirmance of eligibility for certain claims and of the infringement and damages findings validates enforcement of patents covering advances in digital communication standards, supporting patentees in the telecommunications space.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing communication standards face continued patent infringement exposure. The vacatur of eligibility for some claims creates uncertainty about the patentability of constellation design innovations, potentially requiring further litigation on remand.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's phrase 'survives the EPR,' or whether the dispute is purely a state-law contract interpretation issue.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a dispute about whether T-Mobile owed an additional payment under a patent settlement agreement contingent on whether asserted claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination. The court determined the case involved state-law contract interpretation that did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question, and transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit.
impacts.positiveImplications: Clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for patent settlement disputes, ensuring that contract interpretation questions arising from patent settlements are adjudicated in the appropriate regional circuit rather than automatically funneled to the Federal Circuit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements with contingent payment provisions tied to PTO proceedings face potential jurisdictional uncertainty and the risk of forum-shopping disputes, increasing litigation costs when disagreements arise over settlement terms.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the asserted claims of a patent directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants were anticipated by prior art, and whether the accused drug-eluting coronary stent systems infringed those claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict finding infringement and rejecting invalidity, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL of both invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of the University of Texas's patent covering drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in stent systems. The decision overturned a damages award and mooted the cross-appeal on willfulness.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device manufacturers benefit from the reversal, which removes the threat of damages for drug-eluting stent products and narrows the enforceability of university-held patents covering biodegradable polymer drug delivery technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and technology transfer offices face a setback, as the court's willingness to overturn a jury verdict on both anticipation and non-infringement demonstrates the high bar for enforcing broad composition claims in the medical device space.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 after dismissing a patent infringement complaint as futile.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend and the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees to Volkswagen under § 285, finding the case exceptional. The court also addressed sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The decision reinforces accountability for filing frivolous patent infringement suits, particularly where pre-suit damages require adequate pleading of notice.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from strong precedent supporting fee awards and sanctions against frivolous patent suits, deterring speculative patent infringement claims and holding both plaintiffs and their counsel financially accountable.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face heightened risk of fee-shifting and sanctions if infringement complaints are inadequately pleaded, particularly regarding pre-suit notice requirements for damages claims.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation imposing a 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in an antidumping duty sunset review conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on such a deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and upheld Commerce's regulatory 15-day filing deadline for domestic interested parties to express willingness to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews. The court found the statute silent on deadlines and Commerce's regulation a permissible exercise of delegated authority through reasoned decisionmaking. This preserves Commerce's procedural framework for conducting five-year sunset reviews of antidumping duty orders.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers and producers benefit from clear, enforceable procedural deadlines that maintain the integrity of the antidumping duty review process, ensuring that sunset reviews proceed efficiently and that protective duties are not prematurely revoked.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic interested parties who miss the 15-day regulatory deadline risk losing the ability to participate in sunset reviews, potentially leading to revocation of antidumping duty orders that protect them from unfairly priced imports.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade erred in sustaining Commerce's determination—made under protest after remand—that debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit to a foreign steel producer.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and reinstated Commerce's original determinations that debt-to-equity conversions by the Korean government conferred countervailable subsidies on Dongbu Steel. The court held that the trial court improperly sustained Commerce's under-protest determination and directed reinstatement of Commerce's original subsidy findings, supporting imposition of countervailing duties on subsidized imports.
impacts.positiveImplications: U.S. domestic steel producers benefit from reinstatement of countervailing duty determinations, which protect against imports subsidized through government-directed debt-to-equity conversions, preserving fair competitive conditions in the U.S. market.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign producers and importers face reinstated countervailing duties, increasing costs of imported steel products and potentially disrupting established supply chains that relied on the remand determination of no countervailable benefit.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a communications apparatus using a transformer with a non-magnetic core to match impedance for wireless transmission were invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), despite surviving an indefiniteness challenge.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the final judgment of invalidity of Satius's patent claims against Samsung, but on enablement rather than indefiniteness grounds. While reversing the district court's indefiniteness ruling, the court held the claims invalid because the specification did not enable the full scope of the claimed invention. This demonstrates the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds raised by the appellee.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringement benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds, providing multiple avenues to challenge overbroad patent claims even when the district court's primary invalidity theory is reversed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk of invalidity findings on grounds not relied upon by the trial court, as appellate courts may reach alternative invalidity theories raised by the accused infringer, creating uncertainty about patent enforceability.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on both improper venue and patent eligibility (§ 101) grounds simultaneously, or whether the court must stop after dismissing for improper venue.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dual dismissal on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds. The court rejected AML's argument that once the court concluded venue was improper, it lacked authority to also rule on patent eligibility. This permits district courts to resolve substantive patent validity questions even in cases where venue is improper, potentially creating preclusive effects.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain § 101 eligibility rulings even when venue is improper, potentially precluding the same patent claims from being asserted in a different venue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that filing in an improper venue results not only in dismissal but also in a substantive invalidity ruling that could have preclusive effect in subsequent litigation, amplifying the consequences of venue selection errors.
